title: A Stroll Through Georgetown - In Person

title: SHOUT
desc: Join our ensemble of performers as they sing, dance, and teach through storytelling. Learn about the ring shout—a powerful practice blending song and rhythmic movement created by enslaved communities in the 1700s and 1800s. They combined various religious practices of Europe and Africa, creating a cultural tradition that became iconically American. Connect their syncopated musical rhythms from the past to the present and learn how music can be a form of joyful resistance in times of oppression.

title: Before Baker Street: Joseph Bell and the Making of Sherlock Holmes
desc: Sherlock Holmes is known the world over, yet the man Arthur Conan Doyle credited as Sherlock’s prototype is unsung. The deductive powers of 19th-century doctor Joseph Bell—who read patients’ ailments, occupation, and personal habits at a single glance—had a profound influence on medical student Conan Doyle. Author Lindsey Fitzharris recounts how Bell’s work took him from ward to witness box as a medical detective.

title: Pinacoteca Nazionale di Bologna

Among its treasures are masterpieces by Giotto, Raphael, and Parmigianino, as well as of the Bolognese school. Italian Renaissance art expert Rocky Ruggiero discusses the significance of this extraordinary collection and the enduring legacy of Bologna’s artistic tradition. (World Art History Certificate elective, 1/2 credit)

title: The Geology of Yellowstone: Past, Present and Future

He guides participants through the park’s geology, from unique rocks to hydrothermal features, using Google Earth views, diagrams, maps, and field photos to reveal how ongoing volcanic and geothermal forces shape Yellowstone’s dramatic landscape.

title: How to be a Jewish Adult
desc: Do you ever feel like you could use a handbook for how to build a Jewish life? If you identify as Jewish or Jew-ish but aren’t sure how to incorporate Judaism into your day-to-day life, this 8-week series led by guest Rabbi Loren Berman offers equal parts community-building and deep-dive into core lessons from our tradition to help you feel more Jewishly connected.

title: How to Read a Film
desc: Humanities scholar Clay Jenkinson reminds viewers that films are built from thousands of creative choices, and understanding them means examining elements like pace, music, lighting, direction, acting styles, and editing. Learning to isolate these components deepens appreciation without diminishing enjoyment. Jenkinson illustrates his approach through two films from Christopher Nolan, Oppenheimer and The Odyssey, and Philip Kaufman's The Right Stuff .

title: The Language of 1776
desc: In 1776, Americans were not only fighting for political independence but also creating the conditions for new, distinctly American ways of speaking. Linguist Anne Curzan explores the state of the English language in the richly multilingual context of 18th-century America. Curzan traces the birth of Americanisms such as maize , backwoods , and bluff . She also illustrates how patterns of immigration shaped the American accents and dialects heard across regions and social groups today.

title: The Great Harry Houdini: Life, Death, and the Afterlife
desc: The death-defying escapes and daredevil stunts of Harry Houdini made him a sensation. But he created a new role for himself as an anti-spiritualist crusader in his later years, believing that so-called mediums who professed to make contact with the spirits of the departed were hucksters. Author Daniel Stashower explores Houdini’s life and legacy, while actors Scott Sedar and Bari Biern give voice to his career both onstage and in the séance room.

title: The Promised Land: Text, Tradition, and Interpretation
desc: INSIGHTS & IDEAS: TUESDAY NIGHT LEARNING WITH GIDEON AMIR August 4, 11, 18, 25 | 7-8:30 PM ET Location: Zoom Classroom God promised Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob that their descendants would inherit the land of Canaan. After the Exodus from Egypt and forty years of wandering in the desert, the Israelites, under Joshua’s leadership, conquered the Promised Land and settled there. However, the biblical text raises difficult geographical and ethical questions. Join us to explore these questions and examine how they have been understood and addressed across generations.

title: From Alliance to Friendship: Blacks, Jews and Pluralistic Peoplehood

Drawing on their story, Dr. Weinfeld offers a new framework for imagining Black-Jewish relations, one focused on friendship rather than alliance. title: Henri Matisse: An Enduring Fascination
desc: Henri Matisse is considered one of the most innovative and influential artists of the 20th century. Matisse’s oeuvre includes a wide range of materials and styles, but he is best-known for sensual, motion-infused canvases that pulsate with the intense light and vivid color of southern France. Art historian Nancy G. Heller examines these canvases and provides examples of how the artist’s work continues to fascinate. (World Art History Certificate elective, 1/2 credit)

title: The American Colonies in the Age of Sail
desc: In the early 18th century, American colonists along the seaboard built and sailed small vessels in coastal trade. Growing Caribbean plantations needed provisions, prompting widespread smuggling that violated British, French, and Spanish mercantilist laws. Skilled American mariners, adept in shallow-water navigation, became ideal illicit traders. Historian Carl Herzog of the USS Constitution Museum argues that decades of defying imperial policies fostered professional networks, business savvy, and covert practices that ultimately helped sail colonists toward revolution.

title: Hidden Terrors in America: The 1830s Cholera Pandemic
desc: From 1832 to 1836, cholera swept through U.S. cities, towns, farms, prisons, and plantations, killing victims within hours and baffling Americans who lacked bacteriology. Though it struck all classes and regions, elites insisted it targeted only the supposedly immoral, blaming deaths among enslaved African Americans, Indigenous peoples, and Irish immigrants. As fatalities mounted, the universal threat became undeniable. Historian Paul Kelton reveals how this deadly germ collided with the social injustices of the era.

Presented by: Dr. Colleen Brown , Aquatic Ecologist, Sea Grant Knauss Fellow Photo by Colleen Brown

title: Night Photography in Washington, D.C.
desc: Learn the techniques required to capture great nighttime photos, including how to use exposure modes, exposure compensation, white balance, and ISO. title: Orchids: Rooted in History
desc: Orchids aren’t just beautiful—they’re ancient survivors, with a lineage stretching back more than 120 million years. Over time, they’ve adapted to nearly every environment, evolving extraordinary forms and captivating people across cultures. Barb Schmidt , the vice president of the American Orchid Society, leads a journey through deep time, from orchids that grew alongside dinosaurs to the dazzling varieties of today. Schmidt explores their evolution, stories of daring orchid hunters, and the cultural meanings that have made these blooms so fascinating.

title: The Statue of Liberty: A Transatlantic Story
desc: When French sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi first traveled to the United States to propose the construction of a giant tribute to liberty, Americans either rejected the idea or were baffled by it. Nevertheless, completed in 1886, the Statue of Liberty stands today as one of the best-known symbols of the United States. It was ultimately a gift from the French people to the American people, as private citizens, not the two governments, financed it from torch to toe. Historian Edward Berenson illuminates the origins of Lady Liberty, the complex construction process, and her shifting meaning.

title: Franklin D. Roosevelt and the Rise of Fascism
desc: Historian and author William I. Hitchcock argues that Americans were not simply indifferent to the rise of fascism before World War II. From Mussolini’s rise in 1922 to Pearl Harbor in 1941, the nation engaged in intense debates over the threat—and appeal—of authoritarianism. Initially focused on the New Deal and avoiding foreign conflicts, Franklin D. Roosevelt gradually recognized fascism’s dangers. Influenced by journalists, advisers, and activists, he helped build a coalition committed to defending democracy, human rights, and freedom worldwide.

title: Chinese Art: From the Bronze Age to the People’s Republic
desc: With a dynamic, far-reaching history that spans the Neolithic period to the modern age, Chinese civilization has given rise to some of the world’s most remarkable artistic creations. Art historian Robert DeCaroli explores this complex legacy by examining how shifts in China’s social, religious, and political life have influenced transformations in its material culture. title: How to be a Jewish Adult
desc: Do you ever feel like you could use a handbook for how to build a Jewish life? If you identify as Jewish or Jew-ish but aren’t sure how to incorporate Judaism into your day-to-day life, this 8-week series led by guest Rabbi Loren Berman offers equal parts community-building and deep-dive into core lessons from our tradition to help you feel more Jewishly connected.

title: Magna Graecia: Early Greek Culture in Italy
desc: In Plato’s time the South of Italy was known as “Greater Greece,” the beautiful land settled in the centuries after 800 B.C.E. by colonists from the Greek mainland. Author Ross King examines how these settlers brought trade and prosperity as well as their religion, customs, alphabet, and language. They also nurtured on Italian soil the political, philosophical, and artistic foundations that would influence and support the world of the Ancient Romans and, much later, that of the Italian Renaissance.

title: A History of Gilbraltar
desc: In classical antiquity, Gibraltar inspired the original idea that the Earth was divided into distinct continents. Sailors, poets, and geographers saw Gibraltar as a natural marker separating the Mediterranean from the Atlantic and Europe from Africa. This idea had lasting global ramifications, and the geography of the Strait of Gibraltar helped create the pattern of European imperialism and the trajectory of the slave trade. This tour guides you through the exceptional selection of masterpieces, including a striking Syrian-Egyptian basin inlaid with silver figures, an enigmatic Andalusian bronze lion, and a monumental portrait of a Persian king covered with jewels. Meanwhile, learn about the extraordinary journeys these works took and how they were invested with power and new meaning along the way. Image: Signed by Muham

title: Musical Innovation in the Age of AI
desc: Throughout history, new technologies have changed the ways people create, experiment, and bring ideas to life. Today, AI is becoming another tool in the creative process, giving songwriters new ways to improvise, explore possibilities, and develop variations on their ideas. What happens to the creative process when people collaborate with AI? How might new technologies change what it means to compose, invent, and create? In this free public program, a human-centered composer and an expert in computational creativity join a music journalist and critic to explore how AI is reshaping songwriting

title: Basically Jewish
desc: In this five-week course, Rabbi Jenna leads an experiential introduction to Judaism course designed for those looking to reconnect with Judaism, as well as non-Jews looking to discover. This course allows students to develop a deeper connection with the Jewish faith through a digestible, experiential introduction to Jewish traditions, customs, and rituals.

title: By Illegitimate Means: How Birth Decides Dynasties
desc: Legitimacy in medieval and early modern England was never private. Birthright could reorder kingdoms and spark wars. Historian Cheryl White traces how disputed heirs shaped dynasties—from William the Conqueror, mocked as “the Bastard” yet able to seize a throne, to the crises after Edward III and the tenuous claim of Henry VII. White reveals how the fate of a kingdom could turn on one enduring question: Who was born to rule?

title: Gaudí's Vision: Heritage, Innovation, and the Future of Design
desc: As the world commemorates the 100th anniversary of Antoni Gaudí's death, explore the lasting influence of this visionary architect. Most of Gaudi’s Modernist designs are in or near Barcelona, Spain, and seven of them have been named UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Amilcar Vargas , head of heritage at Casa Batlló—a Gaudi masterpiece and UNESCO World Heritage Site—examines how the architect’s work inspires conversations about creativity, sustainability, craftsmanship, and the relationship between nature and the built environment. (World Art History Certificate elective, 1/2 credit)

title: Virunga National Park
desc: The mist-enshrouded peaks of the Virunga Mountains, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, are part of one of Africa’s earliest protected natural areas. Known for an active chain of volcanoes, Virunga National Park is home to the endangered mountain gorilla and more than 300 other faunal and floral species. Historian Justin M. Jacobs shows how together with the adjacent lands of Volcanoes National Park, made famous by the fieldwork of zoologist Dian Fossey, Virunga provides a tense yet majestic backdrop for the competing demands of economic development and ecological preservation.

title: Wexler Lecture on Jewish History: EntryPointDC Happy Hour
desc: Get to the Wexler Lecture a little early for a pre-show happy hour! Grab a mulled cider, hot chocolate, beer, or wine and hang out with other 20-40-somethings before the program begins. Don't forget to RSVP separately for the lecture itself – free to attend, but we need to know how many people to expect. If you have any questions, please reach out to Sarah at sfredrick@edcjcc.org.

title: Sophia Bush
desc: In And I Will Tell You Mine , the activist and actress—known for her roles in “One Tree Hill” and “Chicago P.D.”—shares stories about what has most shaped her: her childhood in Los Angeles, the unexpected road from journalism student to actor, navigating Hollywood and the realities of marriage and divorce.

title: San Francisco: Then and Now
desc: Regional historian and master storyteller John Martini brings the past vividly into the present through the fascinating art of rephotography—the process of locating the exact vantage points of historic photographs and capturing those same scenes today. Using dozens of compelling “then-and-now” comparisons, Martini reveals how some of the Bay Area’s most famous landmarks, including Alcatraz Island, Fort Point, and Sutro Baths, have evolved across more than a century of dramatic change.

title: The American Table: 10 Cookbooks That Shaped a Nation
desc: Among the thousands of cookbooks published since the nation’s earliest days, a select few have transformed the way Americans cook, eat, and think about food. Cultural historian Leslie Goddard journeys through the pages of some of America’s most influential cookbooks, including ones by Fannie Farmer, Irma Rombauer, and Julia Child, and uncovers what they reveal about the evolution of American food culture.

title: Historically Speaking – Loving the Fire: An Evening with Deborah Santana
desc: Join us for an intimate, uplifting evening with Deborah Santana in the Oprah Winfrey Theater. Deborah Santana is a celebrated author, business leader, and founder of Do a Little, a nonprofit dedicated to expanding educational and health opportunities for women and girls globally. Santana is the author of Space Between Stars , co-editor of All the Women in My Family Sing , and producer of five documentary films. It’s designed for curious learners at any stage: whether you’ve never studied Judaism before, want a refresher on what you learned in Hebrew School, or fall somewhere in between. title: The Wexler Lecture on Jewish History: Jews and Christmas, the Untold Story
desc: Today, many American Jews mark December 25th with a familiar ritual: Chinese food and a movie. But just a few hundred years ago, Yiddish-speaking Jews in Europe spent Christmas Eve feasting, drinking, dancing, and gambling. Jordan Chad, author of Christmas in Yiddish Tradition: The Untold Story offers the surprising argument that while Jews never celebrated the birth of Jesus, Christmas did not become the strictly Christian holiday we know today until Jews started migrating to the New World. title: A History of the Movie Musical
desc: As soon as movies learned to talk, they also learned to sing and dance—and the movie musical quickly became one of America’s most popular film genres. Media historian Brian Rose guides you through the rich history of the movie musical, illustrated with extended clips from dozens of classic films. From 42nd Street and Swing Time to Meet Me in St. Louis, West Side Story, and Chicago , the four-part series celebrates the songs, stars, and stories that made movie musicals an enduring part of American culture.

title: J.M.W. Turner and John Constable: Rivals in the Romantic Era
desc: J.M.W. Turner and John Constable, two of Britain’s greatest painters, were contemporaries. While they had very different approaches to their work, their shared belief in the natural world as inspiration and a source of imagination is reflected in their paintings. Art historian Bonita Billman looks at the lives, careers, and oeuvre of Turner and Constable, examining their artistic influences, painting methods, patrons, and personal interests. (World Art History Certificate elective, 1/2 credit)

title: Joseph Smith: The Rise and Fall of an American Prophet

He built temples, created a city-state, ran for president, and practiced plural marriage. Historian John G. Turner traces Smith’s rise from impoverished farmhand to his mob-killing, showing how he forged a religious tradition that continues to resonate widely.

title: Take a Seat!: Chairs of the 20th Century
desc: Many of the chairs still in use today were designed in the 20th century—and have stood the test of time for their comfort, function, and striking visual presence. Art historian Jennie Hirsh explores the history of iconic modern chairs from around the world, tracing how designers including Elaine Gray, Mies van der Rohe, Eero Saarinen, and Charles and Ray Eames reimagined seating for a rapidly changing century. title: The Art of Historic Preservation
desc: Historic preservation is often thought of as the stewardship of grand landmarks associated with great figures like Thomas Jefferson, as well as places of worship, courthouses, and monuments. But the modest houses, working landscapes, and overlooked spaces that hold our personal and collective memories also matter. Public historian Ken Turino traces the history of the preservation movement in America, including how the field has evolved to have a more inclusive vision of what deserves protection.

desc: Enjoy a fall morning walk on a natural oasis in the Potomac River with Melanie Choukas-Bradley , the author of Finding Solace at Theodore Roosevelt Island . The nearly 2-mile path follows Theodore Roosevelt Island’s shore and moves deep into the swamp and tidal inlet along the boardwalk where willows, bald cypresses, and cattails frame views of Washington, D.C. Choukas-Bradley gives an overview of the landscape’s mix of trees, wildflowers, birds, and other wildlife and highlights the island’s history and the legacy of the conservationist president it memorializes.

The cabin is one of two remaining slave dwellings on Edisto Island. Its story provides a revealing glimpse into the most formative and troubling chapters in American history.

title: Big Objects, Big Stories: The Paradox of the Liberty

Talk with a museum docent and explore the tension between slavery and freedom—who belongs and who is excluded. Consider how this paradox resonates through the nation’s history and spurs the American people to wrestle constantly with building “a more perfect Union.”

title: Shtürmer, Rasputin, and the Russian Revolution From Within
desc: In 1917, the Bolsheviks seized power after more than a year of unrest and Russia’s disastrous involvement in World War I. In 1916, Prime Minister Boris Shtürmer had raised the prospect of a separate peace with Germany to support his aspirations to power, and with Rasputin’s help, he contrived to stir up a crisis he could control. Historian and documentarian Indy Neidell examines the facts and myths behind these claims. Before any plan could succeed, however, Rasputin was dead, Shtürmer was imprisoned, and Russia plunged into revolution.

title: The Rise and Fall of Excommunication in Medieval England
desc: Excommunication was originally intended as a severe, rarely imposed punishment that excluded offenders from the sacraments, society, and certain legal rights. Over time, however, it became a routine tool used for political, legal, and personal ends. Historian Charlotte Whatley argues that English bishops increasingly relied on excommunication to resist royal authority, provoking conflict with King Edward III. The Crown ultimately weakened its coercive power, reinforcing the supremacy of English common law.

title: A History of the Movie Musical
desc: As soon as movies learned to talk, they also learned to sing and dance—and the movie musical quickly became one of America’s most popular film genres. Media historian Brian Rose guides you through the rich history of the movie musical, illustrated with extended clips from dozens of classic films. From 42nd Street and Swing Time to Meet Me in St. Louis, West Side Story, and Chicago , the four-part series celebrates the songs, stars, and stories that made movie musicals an enduring part of American culture.

title: Step into the World of M.C. Escher
desc: Maurits Cornelis Escher (1898–1972), popularly referred to as M.C. Escher, is known for what he called his “mental images,” which connect to mathematics and various branches of science. During his 50-year career, Escher’s works evolved from realistic observations of the world to inventions of his imagination that explored multidimensional alternate realities. Dena M. Woodall , a curator at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, explores how Escher’s imagery transformed over time. (World Art History Certificate elective, 1/2 credit)

title: Tours | Arts of China
desc: Examine the diverse artistic and cultural traditions of one of the world’s oldest civilizations in this in-person, docent-led tour. Learn about Chinese artworks such as ritual bronze vessels, calligraphy, brush paintings in ink and color, and exquisite ceramics. Please meet at the West Building Information Desk for the tour. title: Threads of the Viking World: Women’s Lives in Cloth and Craft
desc: A lost mitten. Names carved into spindle whorls. A carefully mended dress laid to rest in a grave. These small, evocative traces open a window into the everyday lives of Viking Age women—lives often missing from the historical record. Historian and broadcaster Eleanor Barraclough draws on archaeological discoveries to reveal the skills, relationships, and identities of women who helped shape the Viking world.

title: Meditation and Mindfulness
desc: Register to join the sessions . Join a free online guided meditation. In these 30-minute sessions, DC-based meditation teachers lead a variety of mindfulness practices. title: Permanent Collection Tour
desc: The National Museum of Asian Art has over 46,000 artworks from across Asia. Enjoy some of the finest on a docent-led tour and learn about commonalities and differences in cultures, aesthetics, and ideas.

title: Tour | From the Louvre
desc: In From the Louvre: Masterpieces of Islamic Art , you can admire remarkable artworks created between the seventh and nineteenth centuries from a vast geographic area extending from Spain to India. This tour guides you through the exceptional selection of masterpieces, including a striking Syrian-Egyptian basin inlaid with silver figures, an enigmatic Andalusian bronze lion, and a monumental portrait of a Persian king covered with jewels. Meanwhile, learn about the extraordinary journeys these works took and how they were invested with power and new meaning along the way. Image: Signed by Muham

title: Conservation Cart Talk | Preparing Art for Display
desc: The same techniques museums use to care for artwork can help protect treasured items at home. Join paper conservator Kesha Talbert for a behind-the-scenes look at how conservators prepare works on paper for display. Learn about conservation-friendly approaches for displaying photographs, prints, and documents, and see how professional practices can be adapted for personal keepsakes. desc: Taverns and coffeehouses have always been more than places to enjoy a drink. As we celebrate the commemoration of America’s 250th anniversary, we’ll explore the role of taverns and coffeehouses as democratic spaces of civic life, hubs of economic development, and centers of regional and local identity. 83rd National Folk Festival
desc: Founded in 1934, the National Folk Festival is the longest-running multicultural celebration of the traditional arts in the United States. The flagship program of the National Council for the Traditional Arts, this traveling festival celebrates the artistic traditions of all Americans and honors the nation’s finest traditional artists. In residence in Jackson, Mississippi, from 2025 to 2027, “the National” features over 300 artists on six stages, nonstop music and dance, parades, a Mississippi folklife area, a family area, regional and international cuisine, and a crafts marketplace.

This session delves into the laws and customs of burial and explores other options the Jewish have chosen in more recent times.
